paper_title: Spatial Harness: Grounding Spatial Reasoning in Executable World States with Physics Engines

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Spatial-Harness

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Spatial reasoning requires vision-language models (VLMs) to infer spatial relations beyond those directly observed in the input views [17, 14]. Determining what lies behind an observer after turn, for example, entails recovering the scene layout and evaluating object relations in the transformed reference frame. Despite advances in multimodal reasoning [15, 27, 7, 26], this remains challenging: GPT-5 achieves 47.59% accuracy on MindCube, compared with 32.35% for random guessing [17]. The difficulty is that direct reasoning leaves both scene representation and spatial transformation within the model (Figure 1, top). VLM may infer an incorrect layout and reason consistently from it, or infer the layout correctly but misapply the requested transformation. The final answer alone cannot distinguish these failures, and fluent explanation provides no independent check of either step. Additional views, as generated by MindJourney [23], provide visual evidence but do not by themselves enforce consistency between scene estimates and subsequent spatial transformations. Our central premise is that scene representation should determine the consequences of spatial operations. An explicit world state makes estimated objects, poses, and relations inspectable, but providing these facts as text still leaves their consequences to model-internal reasoning. Making the state executable instead allows an engine to compute measurements and render views from the specified geometry (Figure 1, bottom). Successive operations then share common scene, against which the model can check its spatial judgments. Execution does not eliminate perceptual uncertainty, but it makes the assumed layout and the results of operations separately available for inspection. We introduce Spatial Harness, which implements this principle with Perceiver and Reasoner in MuJoCo [16]. The Perceiver integrates specialized visual estimates with constraints stated in the question, including camera movements that relate observations across views, to place objects and cameras in shared coordinate frame. The Reasoner queries the instantiated state through Python, using viewpoint changes, geometric measurements, and rendered views to resolve the question. Language constraints and visual geometry jointly define the scene used for spatial computation. Figure 2 presents concrete example: determining what lies behind an observer after 180 turn. After executing the turn, the first rendering shows window ahead, whereas the question asks what is behind. The Reasoner therefore performs another 180 turn to inspect that direction, identifies the grey-green decorative wall, and selects C. With identical GT layouts, Spatial Harness outperforms Base on every backbone, demonstrating gains from executing the supplied layout. Holding the world state fixed allows us to evaluate reasoning independently of scene estimation. Figure 3 compares Base (the same VLM answering without external tools) and Spatial Harness with and without ground-truth (GT) maps specifying object and camera positions and headings. GT maps do not consistently improve Base, but Spatial Harness benefits from executing operations on the supplied state. With Qwen3.5-27B, the same layout yields 71.81% accuracy with Base and 98.25% with Spatial Harness, so the gain cannot be attributed to better scene estimate. Our contributions are as follows: Executable world states. We connect inspectable scene estimates to computed spatial consequences through an explicit interface for spatial reasoning grounded in geometry (Section 3.1). Spatial Harness. We integrate language constraints and visual estimates into shared world state and support interactive reasoning with measurements and rendered views (Sections 3.23.3). Controlled evaluation. We evaluate four benchmarks, compare reasoning with matched states (Figure 3), and analyze scene construction, execution feedback, and state quality (Sections 45).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning. ReAct, ViperGPT, and VisProg organize reasoning around external actions or executable programs [24, 15, 6]. DeepEyes and THYME learn visual tool use [27, 7, 26], while agent frameworks develop planning and verification [11, 29, 30]. These approaches chiefly concern how tools are selected, invoked, and coordinated during reasoning. Spatial Harness complements such orchestration by specifying the geometric state shared by spatial tools, so successive calls return measurements and views derived from the same explicit and inspectable scene assumptions. Spatial Reasoning in VLMs. SpatialVLM, Visual Spatial Tuning, and SpatialRGPT enhance spatial understanding through training or geometric inputs [1, 21, 3]. SpatialPIN and APC construct spatial priors or scene abstractions with visual experts [13, 9]. Among tool-based methods, pySpatial executes programs over reconstructed 3D geometry [12], while GCA constrains computation by formalizing the querys reference frame and objective [2]. Spatial Harness uses question-stated object relations and camera motions to constrain the estimated world state itself. These constraints determine the scene layout, rather than only the reference frame used to query it. Simulation-Grounded Reasoning. MindJourney synthesizes additional viewpoints with video world model [23]. Minds Eye simulates physical outcomes from textual descriptions [10], and LLMPhy estimates physical parameters and layouts through simulation feedback [4]. Spatial Harness uses physics engine for spatial measurements and viewpoint rendering over an estimated static scene. Its world state specifies object and camera geometry, so these queries require neither physical parameter estimation nor prediction of object dynamics. 3 Figure 4: Overview of Spatial Harness. The Perceiver combines question-derived constraints with specialized visual estimates, aligning camera frames and fusing observations into JSON world state = (L, Ω, C): shared layout, per-view observations, and stated constraints. The Reasoner instantiates in MuJoCo and issues Python tool calls for viewpoint control, measurement, and rendering. Computed measurements and rendered views update its context and guide subsequent operations and the final answer. The JSON and code are illustrative excerpts.

sections.title: 3.1 Executable World States for Grounded Reasoning
sections.content: Problem formulation. We consider spatial question answering. Each instance consists of set of images = {Ii}m i=1 of scene with 1, textual query that poses the question and may describe part of the scene, and ground-truth answer Y. model takes (x, q) and predicts ˆy Y. Answering involves two steps: perception, which establishes the scene facts that the question depends on, such as where the entities are and from where each image was taken, and reasoning, which derives the answer from these facts, for example by working out how the scene looks from another viewpoint. VLM that answers directly from (x, q) carries out both steps within one generation. The perceived facts are not represented separately from the reasoning, so an error in perception cannot be told apart from an error in reasoning, and neither step can be checked or improved on its own. Spatial Harness separates the two steps: it makes the perceived facts explicit as world state and grounds the reasoning in computation on that state, so that every spatial judgment, such as what viewpoint change brings into view, is computed by physics engine from the state rather than produced by the VLM. The two steps can then be checked and improved separately. World state. world state is an explicit representation of the scene facts that depends on. Let = {oj}n j=1 denote the entities that involves; the state covers these entities and the properties the question depends on, namely their spatial configuration and that of the cameras, rather than the whole scene. We require the state to be executable: it specifies the geometry concretely enough that geometric quantities, such as the distance between two entities, the direction of an entity from chosen viewpoint, or the view from camera placed anywhere in the scene, can be computed from it. The world state has two levels: the observations from each image, and the arrangement of all entities and cameras in one scene (Figure 5). The observation level holds what each image shows: Ωi lists the entities visible in Ii with their direction, distance, and facing relative to camera i, measured metrically or described qualitatively. Observations from different images are expressed relative to different cameras and can be related to each other only once the camera poses are known. The layout level places all entities and cameras in single coordinate system, which we call the shared frame: gives the position and heading (pj, θj) of every entity and (ci, ϕi) of every camera, obtained by aligning the observations through the camera poses, and it is the part that is instantiated for computation. The constraints collect the scene facts stated in q, such as relation between two entities or between two viewpoints; they hold exactly and apply to both levels. The observation level is kept alongside the layout because the alignment can lose or distort what an individual image shows, and the Reasoner can consult the observations directly. The world state is thus = (L, Ω, C) with Ω = {Ωi}m Decoupling perception from reasoning. The perceived facts are thereby exposed in ˆs for inspection and evaluation, and the reasoning is grounded: the consequences of spatial operations are computed by the engine from ˆs rather than generated by the VLM. The next two sections describe them.

sections.title: 3.2 Perceiver: Estimating the World State
sections.content: The Perceiver estimates ˆs from (x, q) (Figure 4, middle). The query determines which entities and properties the state must contain and may state some of the facts, whereas the images are the source of the observations and the camera poses. text channel and visual channel process the two inputs, for one image or several alike, and compilation turns their outputs into the layout. Text channel. VLM parses into four kinds of information. The entities are the objects and viewers the question involves. The relations are facts that states about pairs of entities, such as one being to the left of another. The viewpoints are facts that states about the cameras, such as the camera turning left between two images. The query is the spatial question to be answered together with the types of information it requires, such as direction, distance, facing, or camera motion. Relations and viewpoints, when stated, form and constrain the layout and the camera poses; the required information types later decide whether ˆs can support the answer (Section 3.3). Visual channel. The visual channel estimates Ωi for each image and the relative poses of the cameras when there are multiple images. It applies specialized models in four steps: detection localizes each entity in in the image, which with the camera intrinsics gives its direction; depth estimation gives its distance; orientation estimation gives its facing; and, for multiple images, camera pose estimation gives the rotation and translation between cameras. The VLM also describes each image qualitatively, e.g., which entities are visible and how pairs are ordered, which covers entities the models fail to measure. If no observation relates pair of entities the answer depends on, the Perceiver queries the VLM about this pair directly, so that every relation the question hinges on has at least one source. Compilation. Compilation turns the observations and constraints into the layout. The shared frame is defined by the camera that took the first image I1: this camera is placed at the origin and its viewing direction serves as the reference heading, so (c1, ϕ1) = (0, 0). The poses of the other cameras come from up to four sources: the viewpoints stated in q, the camera pose estimator, the entities seen in common with an earlier image, and the camera motion described by the VLM. We use the sources in fixed order of priority, taking the first one that is available. For the heading, the order is stated viewpoints, common entities, pose estimator, VLM description; for the position, it is stated viewpoints, pose estimator, VLM description. The two components are chosen separately, and component that no source provides remains unknown. Each observation is then projected into the shared frame. sections.title: 3.3 Reasoner: Grounded Reasoning with a Physics Engine
sections.content: The Reasoner instantiates ˆs in the physics engine and answers by querying it (Figure 4, right). Physics engine as tool. MuJoCo [16] scene is built from scene description that gives each body shape, either mesh asset or geometric primitive, and pose. Generating faithful mesh for each entity from the images is beyond what current models do reliably, so each entity is represented by proxy instead: cylinder of fixed size at (pj, θj), with heading marker and the entitys name as its label. Each input image corresponds to camera at (ci, ϕi). The proxies carry exactly the information in the layout, on which the spatial questions depend. The resulting scene is E[ˆs]. The Reasoner operates on it by writing code against tool interface (Figure 6; full signatures in Listing 1), and the engine returns printed results and rendered images. The operations form three groups: Viewpoint control places the camera at given pose, such as the pose of an input image or position described in the question, or moves and rotates it by given distances and angles. The camera keeps its pose between calls, so each operation starts from where the previous one left the camera, and multi-step movement is executed step by step, one call at time. Measurement returns the current camera pose, the distance from the camera to each entity, or the camera motion between two views, i.e., the translation and rotation from one to the other. Rendering returns the current view, with proxies labeled by name and distance. Every result is computed from ˆs, so the feedback is deterministic and consistent with it. Interactive reasoning. With the scene in place, the Reasoner answers in loop with the engine. The context h1 initially holds x, q, ˆs, and description of each operation in the interface, giving its purpose, arguments, and return value. At step t, the Reasoner reads the context, issues an operation at, and receives the feedback ft, i.e., the printed results and, if requested, the rendered view, which is appended to the context together with the operation: at = R(ht), ft = E[ˆs](at), ht+1 = ht (at, ft). (4) In this loop, the Reasoner chooses operations whose results answer the question. For example, to decide whether moving forward brings the observer closer to an entity, it measures the distance before and after the movement; to find what is on the observers left after turn, it performs the turn, faces left, and renders the view. sections.title:
4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate on four spatial reasoning benchmarks: MindCube-Tiny [17], SAT [14], MMSI-Bench [22], and SpatialRGPT-Bench [3]. MindCube-Tiny (MindCube hereafter) contains 1,050 multiple-choice questions over few real-image views, grouped by camera motion into Rotation, Among, and Around. For SAT, we sample 500 questions from its synthetic split, 100 from each of five categories. MMSI-Bench contains 1,000 multiple-choice questions over multiple real-scene images. The quantitative split of SpatialRGPT-Bench contains 749 questions that require numerical estimates. We report answer accuracy on the three multiple-choice benchmarks; on SpatialRGPT-Bench, prediction is correct if it is within the error tolerance. Appendix C.6 provides further details. Baselines. We compare with three baselines: Base, MindJourney [23], and pySpatial [12]. Base prompts the VLM to answer without external tools. MindJourney uses video world model to generate views along camera trajectories proposed by the VLM, which then answers from the generated views. pySpatial lets the VLM write Python programs that call 3D reconstruction, camera-pose, and novelview tools. Appendix D.2 further compares with GCA [2]. Evaluation settings. We evaluate in two settings. The GT-map setting uses the annotated cognitive map that MindCube provides for each question, which gives the ground-truth scene layout; we call it the GT map. It marks the positions and facing directions of the relevant objects and cameras on 10 10 birds-eye-view grid. Base reads the map as text in its prompt, whereas Spatial Harness instantiates the map in the engine and the Reasoner queries it. Because both methods start from the same scene information, this setting compares how they reason with it, separately from errors in state estimation. In the end-to-end setting, methods receive only the images and question. Spatial Harness builds its world state with the Perceiver, and the baselines use their own tools. Vision-language models. All methods in comparison use the same VLM. sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: Reasoning with GT maps. Figure 3 summarizes overall accuracy with and without GT maps. Table 1 reports MindCube accuracy in the GT-map setting. Providing the map for direct reasoning does not always help and can even hurt: with the map, Base accuracy drops from 35.59% to 30.35% with Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Some recent models make better use of the map, which raises Base accuracy by 19.11 points with Qwen3.5-27B and 30.60 points with Kimi K2.5. Spatial Harness instead grounds each reasoning step in engine feedback. With the same map, it reaches 84.22% with Qwen2.5-VL72B and 98.25% with Qwen3.5-27B, 42.76 and 26.44 points above Base with the map. Grounded feedback thus improves reasoning whether or not the textual map helps Base. End-to-end performance. Table 2 reports end-to-end results on MindCube, where Spatial Harness reasons over the world state estimated by its Perceiver. It achieves the highest overall accuracy with all four VLMs, exceeding the strongest baseline, pySpatial, by 5.40 points on average. With Qwen3.5-27B, it reaches 71.14%, 18.44 points above Base and 7.52 points above pySpatial. Spatial Harness differs from the baselines in where its feedback comes from: the world state takes in both the images and the question, and every measurement and rendered view is computed from that state. MindJourney instead imagines new viewpoints with video world model, whose generated views are not constrained by an explicit scene, and it stays within 4.42 points of Base. pySpatial reasons over scene reconstructed from pixels, which cannot capture spatial information given only in the question, such as the camera motion between views, and it falls below Base on some question categories. Table 3 reports end-to-end results on the other three benchmarks. Averaged over the three benchmarks, Spatial Harness achieves the highest accuracy with both models, 15.26 and 14.20 points above the strongest baseline. On SAT, most questions provide single image, and the VLM already answers many of them well. Reconstructing 3D scene from single image is difficult, and pySpatial, which reasons over such reconstructions, falls 13.20 and 13.80 points below Base. Spatial Harness achieves the best accuracy with both models (71.60% and 83.20%). On MMSI-Bench, it improves over Base with Qwen3.5-27B from 33.40% to 39.50%. With Qwen2.5-VL-72B, it remains at the Base level (29.00% vs. 29.60%), because the model often misreads the coordinates in the world state and does not act on the engines feedback in its reasoning. sections.content: World state construction. To examine how the world state should be constructed, we fix the Reasoner and vary the source of the map on MindCube with Qwen3.5-27B  (Table 4)  . In the VLMgenerated condition, the VLM produces the map directly from the images and question without the Perceiver. Accuracy drops from 71.14% to 41.33%: the VLM alone cannot reliably estimate the state, and the Perceivers structured estimation is needed. We then ablate the two perception channels. Without the visual channel, the VLM estimates the geometric fields in place of the specialized visual models, and accuracy drops to 52.95%. Without the text channel, the VLM identifies the relevant entities from the images instead of extracting them from the question, and accuracy drops to 68.38%. Both channels are therefore needed, and the visual channel contributes more. We also ablate the design within each channel (Figure 7). Since the Reasoner works on the world state estimated by the Perceiver, we examine how closely this state matches the scene. We compare the world states that the Perceiver estimates with Qwen3.5-27B against the GT maps of all 1,050 MindCube questions. Following MindCube [17], we score each map with its cognitive-map metrics (Appendix D.5): validity, coverage, and directional and facing similarity. Nearly all estimated maps are valid (99.52%), and they recover 72% of the annotated entities after name alignment (Figure 8). With these maps, Spatial Harness already achieves the best end-to-end accuracy, and its higher accuracy with GT maps suggests that more accurate maps would raise it further; Appendix D.6 measures how accuracy degrades when single fields of the GT map are corrupted. The grounded feedback of the engine could also be used to check the world state itself. The engine can render it from the estimated pose of each input view. rendering that disagrees with the corresponding input image would locate an error for the Perceiver to correct. Directional similarity Facing similarity Coverage Limitations. Our world state describes static scene at single moment, which suffices for the spatial questions in our benchmarks but cannot represent change over time, such as objects moving in video. time dimension is the natural next step: recording the poses of entities and the camera at each frame would let the engine instantiate the scene at any moment and measure how it changes between frames, which would support questions about motion and the order of events. We plan to support this temporal dimension in future work, together with the video benchmarks that require it.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Answering spatial question involves perception, which establishes the scene facts, and reasoning, which can be computed exactly once those facts are explicit. We therefore propose Spatial Harness, which separates the two steps: Perceiver estimates the scene facts from the images and the question as an explicit world state, and Reasoner answers by operating on this state in physics engine, so that every measurement and rendered view is computed from the state rather than imagined. Experiments on four spatial reasoning benchmarks show that Spatial Harness outperforms strong baselines, and ablations attribute the gains to both the explicit state and the grounded feedback. We hope this work encourages the use of physics engines as general substrate for grounding multimodal reasoning about the physical world, where perception and reasoning can be checked separately.

sections.title: A Broader Impacts
sections.content: Spatial Harness may benefit embodied agents by improving spatial reasoning through explicit world states and executable feedback. Making scene interpretations and computed evidence available for inspection could support the development of more reliable and transparent embodied systems. Since errors in scene estimation or reasoning can still affect downstream decisions, applications in physical environments should include appropriate validation.

sections.title: B Use of Large Language Models
sections.content: Vision-language models are core components of Spatial Harness: in each experiment, the evaluated VLM serves as the VLM in the Perceiver and as the Reasoner (Section 3), the baselines use the same VLM, and Section 4.1 lists the models. An LLM judge scores free-form answers against the reference answers (Appendix C.6), and the name judge of the map-quality evaluation is an LLM as well (Appendix D.5). Beyond these roles in the method and the evaluation, LLMs assisted only in preparing the manuscript, where they were used to polish the wording and check the grammar; they did not produce the research ideas, the experiments, or the results. The authors have reviewed the whole text and take full responsibility for its content, including its originality and factual accuracy. No LLM is an author of this paper.

The text channel and the qualitative image descriptions use the evaluated VLM. LocateAnything-3B [19] detects each entity by name, and Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B [25] binds detector 15 labels to entity names when the two do not match exactly. MoGe-2 [18] estimates metric depth and camera intrinsics, and the depth of an entity is the median depth over the central half of its box. Orient Anything V2 [20] estimates the facing direction of an entity in the camera frame, which is kept when its front confidence is at least 0.5. For multiple images, Reloc3r [5] estimates the relative rotation and the translation direction between the first image and each other image. The perception models are served on A100 GPUs. Image descriptions and pair queries. For each image, the VLM reports whether each entity is visible, its coarse horizontal position (left, center, or right), its depth rank, its coarse facing, and the leftright and frontback order of entity pairs. detected box that the VLM does not confirm as visible receives low confidence. When the question names fewer than two entities, the VLM proposes landmarks in each image, which locate the cameras and are placed on the map but do not count as question entities. Pair queries cover at most eight entity pairs for which the image descriptions give no leftright or in-front-of order, starting with the pairs that involve the reference entity of the question. pair visible in one image is queried in that image for its leftright and frontback order; pair seen in different images but never together is queried across two images, and only its leftright order is kept. Camera poses. Each camera pose has three components: two position coordinates and heading. Each source supplies the components it can measure with fixed confidence. For the heading, these are the text (0.95), landmark correspondences between images (0.6), Reloc3r (0.5), and VLM estimate of the motion from the previous image (0.4, capped by the confidence of the previous pose); for the position, the text (0.95), Reloc3r (0.7), and the VLM estimate (0.4, capped likewise). Each component is taken separately from its most confident source, and component that no source measures is marked as unknown, except that camera motion stated in the text sets its omitted displacement components to zero, and stated rotation in place keeps the previous position and its confidence in preference to visual estimates unless the text gives absolute coordinates. The layout uses 10 10 grid, the format of the MindCube cognitive maps; the first camera is placed at the grid center facing up, and the joint camera and entity coordinates are mapped onto the grid by monotone map that keeps interior coordinates and compresses the outlying ones. Each action moves the camera forward by 0.75 or rotates it by 27, and trajectory moves at most 1.5 forward and turns at most 60. Stable Virtual Camera generates 8 views per trajectory with 20 diffusion steps and guidance scale of 4, and each search layer keeps at most 18 helpful views. pySpatial [12] lets the VLM write Python programs that call 3D reconstruction, camerapySpatial. pose, and novel-view tools, and the final answering stage receives the original images together with the program output. D.2 Comparison with GCA GCA [2] formalizes the question as geometric constraints and solves them with geometric tools on scene reconstructed from the images. We run it on MindCube under the same protocol as the end-to-end baselines in Table 2. Table 9 shows that Spatial Harness achieves the highest overall accuracy with both models. Like pySpatial, GCA reasons over scene reconstructed from pixels, which cannot take in facts stated only in the question, such as the camera motion between views. D.3 World State Construction Ablations State source and channel ablations. Table 4 holds the downstream Reasoner fixed and changes the state source. VLM-generated maps are produced directly from the images and question without the two-channel Perceiver (Figure 15); when generated map fails the format check (237 of 1,050 questions), the VLM answers directly from the images and question. Without the text channel, the VLM lists the visible objects from the images without the question, and the relations and camera poses stated in the text are dropped. Without the visual channel, it estimates the visual fields itself while retaining the text channels structured output. Full Perceiver (Spatial Harness) uses both channels; the GT map supplies the annotated-state reference. These conditions distinguish direct map generation from replacing one channel within the structured pipeline. 28 Text-module interventions. Figure 7(a) varies the structured entity-and-relation module and the text-derived camera/view constraints separately, keeping the remaining state-construction stages and Reasoner fixed. The former extracts question-relevant entities and relations; the latter recovers stated camera motion and cross-view constraints. They are separate interventions rather than joint removal of the entire text channel: the first replaces the extracted entities with the objects the VLM lists from the images and drops the stated relations while keeping the camera constraints, and the second drops the camera constraints while keeping the entities and relations. Visual-estimator substitutions. Each condition in Figure 7(b) replaces one specialist with the VLM performing the same task in the same units. The detector replacement supplies regions to the unchanged depth and orientation estimators. Replacing depth, orientation, or relative pose preserves the other estimators. This substitution is necessary because deleting parent output would also disable its dependent stages and measure the loss of an entire branch. D.4 Grounded Feedback Conditions Table 5 uses Qwen3.5-27B and fixed GT map; the conditions differ in the feedback available to the Reasoner and the corresponding interaction protocol. Base answers from the map without engine feedback. Multi-turn self-review makes second pass over the initial answer without new scene information. Numerical feedback only exposes geometric computations without rendered images. Rendered feedback only exposes rendered views after viewpoint changes; distance queries and camera-motion descriptions are removed, and only the camera pose remains readable. Spatial Harness provides both feedback types. These comparisons isolate reasoning over supplied state from errors in state estimation. D.5 World State Quality Metrics Figure 8 evaluates Perceiver maps against the annotations for all 1,050 MindCube questions. The four reported metrics lie in [0, 1]: Validity: the fraction of predicted maps passing the required format checks. Coverage: the fraction of annotated objects and views recovered under name matching. Directional Similarity: the match rate of pairwise directional relations between recovered entities, over the pairs with an annotated relation. Facing Similarity: facing-label accuracy for recovered entities with annotated facing. Figure 8 aligns names before scoring: generated Image and View names are matched to the annotated views, and generated object name is matched one-to-one to an annotated object when an LLM name judge (Qwen3.5-27B) accepts the two names as the same object. As in the official MindCube scorer, the predicted map is compared under the rotation that best aligns it with the annotation. Our implementation reproduces the official scorer (commit 6d8fd9a) on all 1,050 questions. Scores are averaged over all 1,050 questions, and missing or malformed maps remain in the denominator as empty maps. These metrics measure agreement with the annotated map, not continuous metric reconstruction error. The resulting map can pass format checks while omitting entities or assigning incorrect spatial relations. D.6 Sensitivity to State Errors Table 10 corrupts one field type of the GT map at time while holding Qwen3.5-27B and the Reasoner fixed. Starting from GT maps separates the injected error from errors already present in predicted maps. The uncorrupted GT-map condition supplies the reference accuracy. Each condition is run with three corruption seeds (42, 43, 44), and the table reports the mean accuracy. For object position, one object selected by the seed moves by one, two, or three cells along one of the eight grid directions, to free cell inside the grid; the three levels move the same object in the same direction. For camera pose, only the yaw of one view selected by the seed changes, with perturbation magnitudes in (0, 30], (30, 90], or (90, 180] degrees. sections.title: E Case Studies
sections.content: The following MindCube cases, both in the GT-map setting, give complete Reasoner trajectories. Each listing contains the code of every tool call, one block per turn; the text below it describes the Reasoners reasoning and the engine responses, quoting the trajectory. Coordinates and directions follow the grid-map API, in which yaw of 0, 90, 180, and 270 degrees faces right, up, left, and down on the map. Each case is compared with Base, which receives the same images and GT map but no engine. 30 Question: Based on these four images (image 1, 2, 3, and 4) showing the red bottle from different viewpoints (front, left, back, and right), with each camera aligned with room walls and partially capturing the surroundings: From the viewpoint presented in image 4, what is to the left of the red bottle? A. Curtain B. Gray-green tufted backrest C. TV and electric fan D. Wall and door 1 2 4 Figure 19: The success case (item among_group603_q3_5_1). The top shows the question, and the bottom presents the four images, numbered as in the question. The reference answer is B. Success: grounding the viewpoint change in the engine. Figure 19 shows the question and the four images. The question asks: From the viewpoint presented in image 4, what is to the left of the red bottle? The options are A. Curtain; B. Gray-green tufted backrest; C. TV and electric fan; D. Wall and door. In the GT map, the red bottle is at [5, 5], the backrest at [5, 8], the curtain at [2, 5], the TV and fan at [5, 2], the wall and door at [8, 5], and the camera of image 4 at [6, 5] facing left. The trajectory of Qwen3.5-27B (item among_group603_q3_5_1) has two turns and one tool call: # Turn 1 # Set camera to Image 4s position and facing mujoco_sim.set_camera([6, 5], "left") # Turn left to see what is to the left of the bottle from this viewpoint mujoco_sim.turn_left() # Capture the image to identify the object image_path = mujoco_sim.capture_image() Figure 20: View rendered by capture_image() in the first turn of the success case. In the first turn, the Reasoner plans to set the camera to the position and facing of Image 4, turn the camera to the left to look at the area to the left of the bottle, and capture an image to identify the object in that direction. The engine renders the view facing down on the map (yaw 270; Figure 20) 31 and returns the gray-green tufted backrest at distance 3.2 as the only entry of objects_in_view. In the second turn, the Reasoner calls no tool and answers B, stating that the tool captured the view after turning left and identified the gray-green tufted backrest. With the same images and GT map, Base, which reasons directly over the same map without the engine, answers in all three runs. In the first run, it reasons that from the cameras position at [6, 5] looking left towards the bottle at [5, 5], the direction to the left of the bottle corresponds to the direction the camera is facing (further decreasing x-values), and selects the curtain, the object straight ahead. The Reasoner answers in all three runs. The viewpoint change is executed, not imagined: the engine renders the view after the turn, and the answer comes from this grounded feedback rather than from internal imagination. Question: Based on these four images (image 1, 2, 3, and 4) showing the toy train from different viewpoints (front, left, back, and right), with each camera aligned with room walls and partially capturing the surroundings: From the viewpoint presented in image 3, what is to the left of the toy train? A. Window B. Printed glass door C. Black table D. Wall 1 3 4 Figure 21: The failure case (item among_group738_q2_5_1). The top shows the question, and the bottom presents the four images, numbered as in the question. The reference answer is A. Failure: overriding the engines feedback. Figure 21 shows the question and the four images. The question asks: From the viewpoint presented in image 3, what is to the left of the toy train? The options are A. Window; B. Printed glass door; C. Black table; D. Wall. In the GT map, the toy train is at [5, 5], the black table at [5, 8], the wall at [2, 5], the printed glass door at [5, 2], the window at [8, 5], and the camera of image 3 at [5, 4] facing down. The trajectory of Kimi K2.5 (item among_group738_q2_5_1) has four turns and three tool calls: # Turn 1 # Set camera to Image 3s position and facing mujoco_sim.set_camera([5, 4], "down") # From this viewpoint facing down, need to check whats to the left of the toy train # First, let me capture the current view to see the toy train image_path = mujoco_sim.capture_image() print("Objects in view from Image 3:", image_path) # Turn 2 # From Image 3s position facing down, turn right to see whats to the left of the toy train mujoco_sim.set_camera([5, 4], "down") mujoco_sim.turn_right() # This turns towards +x direction (window side) image_path = mujoco_sim.capture_image() print("Objects to the left of toy train from Image 3:", image_path) # Turn 3 # Let me verify by checking both sides from Image 3s position # First, reset to Image 3s position facing down mujoco_sim.set_camera([5, 4], "down") # Turn left to see whats on the other side of the toy train 32 mujoco_sim.turn_left() # This turns towards +x direction (window side) image_path_left = mujoco_sim.capture_image() print("Objects to the right of toy train from Image 3:", image_path_left) # Get distances to confirm distances = mujoco_sim.get_distances() print("Distances after turning left:", distances) Turn Turn 2 Turn 3 Figure 22: Views rendered by capture_image() in the three tool-calling turns of the failure case, in order. In the first turn, the Reasoner reasons that when facing down, left = towards +x (right on grid), so the toy trains left would be towards [8, 5] where the window is, and captures the view of image 3 to verify; the engine returns the toy train at distance 1.0 and the black table at 4.0 (Figure 22, left). In the second turn, it assumes that when facing down, right turn points towards +x and turns right; the engine renders the view facing left on the map (yaw 180; Figure 22, middle) and returns the wall at 3.2. In the third turn, the Reasoner corrects the turn directions, turning right points towards -x and turning left points towards +x, but reinterprets the question: the question asks about the toy trains left, not the cameras left, and the toy trains left would be towards the cameras right (towards -x, which is the wall at [2, 5]), so the answer should be D. Wall. To double-check, it turns left and requests the distances; the engine renders the view facing right on the map (yaw 0; Figure 22, right), returns the window at 3.2, and reports distances of 1.0 to the toy train, 4.0 to the black table, 3.162 to the wall and the window, and 2.0 to the printed glass door. In the fourth turn, the Reasoner calls no tool. It notes that when turned left (towards +x direction), saw the window at distance 3.2, but keeps that the toy trains left side is towards the -x direction (wall side) and answers D. The reference answer is A. The engine executes every call correctly, and the capture after turn_left() in the third turn returns the window. The Reasoners analysis in the first turn also points to the window. In the third turn, however, the Reasoner reinterprets the question in the toy trains own frame, as if the train faced the camera, and keeps this reading in its final turn although it contradicts both its first analysis and the turn-left capture. The final answer coincides with that of Base with the same map, which answers in all three runs, whereas the Kimi K2.5 Reasoner answers in its other two runs and the Qwen3.5-27B Reasoner answers in all three. Grounded feedback shows the correct answer but does not force the model to use it: this failure occurs when the Reasoner sets aside the engines observation in favor of its internal interpretation of the question.

sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and Section 1 state the claims: perception is made explicit as world state, and reasoning is grounded in feedback computed by physics engine. Section 4 supports them on four benchmarks with openand closed-weight VLMs. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Please see Section 5. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not include theoretical results. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 4.1 and Appendix give the benchmarks, models, prompts, and evaluation protocol, and the code is released at https://github.com/tmlr-group/ Spatial-Harness. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code 35 Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The code is publicly available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/ Spatial-Harness, and Appendix describes the implementation and evaluation setup. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/ public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 4.1 gives the experimental settings, and Appendix gives the implementation, decoding, and scoring details. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Please see Table 11. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). 36 The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to library function, bootstrap, etc.) The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report 2-sigma error bar than state that they have 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix C.6 gives the GPUs used for the locally served models; the closedweight models are accessed through APIs. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didnt make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Our paper conforms to the NeurIPS Code. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require deviation from the Code of Ethics. The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Please see Section A. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. 37 Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not have such risks. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. Released models that have high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: For the datasets and open-sourced models that we use in our experiments, we cited the papers that produced them. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include URL. The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. For scraped data from particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. 38 If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of dataset. For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the assets creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] at https://github.com/tmlr-group/ Justification: Spatial-Harness with README that documents installation, configuration, and evaluation, and Appendix gives the implementation details. released code
